title: ACEIT brings the paper-roster case to council
summary: Anoka County Election Integrity Team (ACEIT) educates Oak Grove officials on why paper check-in rosters are lawful, auditable, and under local control—and how electronic poll pads change the information picture on Election Day.
detail: ACEIT deck title: “Achieving Home-Grown Elections in Anoka County.” Erik attended (Simon’s Sensors Ch. 3). Goals include paper poll books under §201.225 and recommended municipal resolutions.

title: Oak Grove votes for paper
summary: City Council adopts Resolution 24-101 (4–0 per ACEIT) to terminate the Anoka electronic-roster agreement and return to paper poll books. Ramsey later cancels after the 2024 election (teaser pin).
detail: Res. 24-101 cites §201.225 (municipality may use e-rosters; not mandated) and gives notice of intent to use paper. Later Res. 2025-032 renews the discontinue path.

title: County letter threatens felonies for paper
summary: Anoka County Elections sends a multi-page unsigned letter to precinct head judges warning that using paper poll pads could mean felony exposure. Later process questions about authorship and signing are labeled as questions, not conclusions.
detail: Library hosts an ODT transcription extract (not the original county PDF). ACEIT/Sensors: Elections Manager Tom Hunt later acknowledged sending it on behalf of Auditor Pam LeBlanc (~6 months later; verbal report to Erik, not a dated transcript).

title: Courts clarify municipal roster choice
summary: In City of Oak Grove v. Simon (A26-0910), the Minnesota Supreme Court holds that under §201.225 the municipality—not the county—decides paper vs electronic voter rosters. Oak Grove may use paper for the Nov 2026 general. Opinion to follow.
detail: UMLC petition (May 2026) opened the path. Aug 11 scheduling order set oral argument for Sept 8. Court expresses no view on prosecuting city staff under §204B.44.

title: Act while paper remains a local option
summary: Compare the 2023 electronic-tabulator lock-in pattern: once statutes harden a practice, local choice shrinks. Councils and citizens who want auditable paper check-in should move while statutes still leave room—and ask auditors for the data that is public. Clearer published data is common ground.
detail: Peers: Ramsey canceled e-pads after 2024; Linwood followed through on paper in 2026. Broader Anoka precinct paper-vs-e list for Nov 2026 is still an open question.
